prize_parts.citation: For discoveries on the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the development of long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I still hold B006 as the sole prize part. All six of us converge on it, but I treat that as a check and not as the argument. The argument is that it is a complete chain from physiology to medicine that has been independently confirmed for decades: Holst on the secretion and action of GLP-1 in humans, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology, receptor signalling and extra-pancreatic actions, and then the half-life extension that turned a peptide lasting minutes into a once-daily or once-weekly drug. The clinical consequence is broad and still widening, covering glycaemic control, weight loss and cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and the central appetite-regulation effects make it as much a neurobiological finding as an endocrine one. I keep Knudsen in the third seat as an explicit choice about what the citation rewards. The change to medicine came from the physiology and from the pharmacology that made it usable, and a citation that names only the first would describe the principle but not what reached patients. I would not call the choice free of cost, since it places an industry scientist on the list and leaves out the earliest peptide-identification work.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the main weakness. Three seats cannot cover Drucker, Holst, Knudsen, Mojsov and Habener, and each omission can be defended as unfair. Choosing Knudsen over Mojsov risks being read as honouring development over the identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide. The members who favour Mojsov, Perlmann and Wahren-Herlenius especially, make a fair point that the tradition of this prize leans toward discovery of a principle, and I cannot show from the supplied material that Knudsen's step is a discovery in that sense and not an optimisation of a known mechanism. Against that, I cannot settle Mojsov's priority against Habener and others from the supplied material, and a contested priority is a weaker foundation for a laureate seat than a decisive and undisputed contribution. Long-term safety and durability of weight loss are also still being characterised, though this does not weaken the discovery.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that the prize should recognise how GLP-1 works as a hormone and its active form, and that analogue engineering is a later, partly proprietary step carried by a large team, so replacing Mojsov with Knudsen shifts the prize toward development.
responses.response: I accept that the analogue work was done by a team and is partly proprietary, and that this is the strongest argument for Mojsov. I do not think it removes Knudsen, because the acylation and albumin-binding design is a specific scientific contribution to why the peptide works in patients, and it is the step that links the hormone to the outcome trials. Where we agree is that the choice must be explicit. If the committee decides the citation is for discovery of the hormone and its active form, I would accept Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and would not block it. I also note your point that attribution cleanness should not be bought at the price of breadth, and I keep B006 as the lead for that reason.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved B006 ahead of B001 and argues that the Mojsov dispute is one among academic scientists about who deserves credit and not about whether the step was necessary, whereas industry credit raises a different question.
responses.response: That is a useful distinction and I agree that necessity is not what is in dispute for Mojsov. It is a reason to take her seat seriously, and it weakens any argument that the identification step is secondary. My reply is that the priority question still bears on the seat. A contested priority is a weaker basis for an award than a role that nobody disputes, and I would want the committee to read the primary record before giving it up. On industry credit I see it as a question of who made the decisive contribution, not of principle, and that is a point I hold only for this configuration. I also take note that you left B001 as an alternative. I still see its cleaner two-person credit as a real strength, but it does not outweigh B006's breadth.

responses.point: El-Manira says that replacing Mojsov with Knudsen turns this into a development prize while the basic-science credit is still being argued, and would accept Drucker, Holst and Knudsen only as the safer choice if the priority record proves unclear.
responses.response: I agree that this is the right frame, and my position is nearly the mirror of yours. You would take Knudsen only if the record is unclear, and I would take Mojsov if the committee explicitly chooses a discovery-only citation. I disagree that Knudsen makes it a development prize. The citation I propose names the physiology first and the therapies second, with two academic physiologists in two of the three seats. If the committee judges that I am underweighting the discovery, the cost to my configuration is small, because Drucker and Holst remain in either case.

responses.point: Sandberg agrees with the Knudsen configuration, says a Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio is defensible, and qualifies my earlier remit argument on optogenetics by noting that methods such as PCR and CRISPR were recognised because they changed what can be discovered.
responses.response: You are right about the remit and I withdraw that argument. A method is not a weaker fit for this prize by itself, and my reservation about B002 is the six-name credit problem and its still early medical effect. A Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel trio omits Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck, and I do not see a fair three-name solution. On the third GLP-1 seat we agree on Knudsen, but I do not want that agreement to count for more than the argument. The strongest counter-argument is Perlmann's, and I do not have a full answer to it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee decides the citation rewards discovery of GLP-1 physiology and its active form or discovery plus development, which settles Mojsov against Knudsen and should be decided explicitly.
Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) peptide relative to Habener and others, which I cannot verify from the supplied material.
Whether crediting an industry scientist is acceptable here as a consequence of the decisive contribution and not a precedent.
For B019, whether Rosenberg's adoptive cell therapy work belongs in a CAR-T citation and how to handle Eshhar and other early originators outside the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the credited names on the shortlist is documented as a collaborator, supervisor or colleague. For transparency, my profile records a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard and about twenty co-authored works with committee member Thomas Perlmann, and neither bears on B006, B019 or B002. My neuropharmacology background gives me a topic interest in the central appetite-regulation effects of GLP-1, which is not a connection to any candidate. This is unchanged from round 1.
